Question: If \(554\) is the base \(b\) representation of the square of the number whose base \(b\) representation is \(24,\) then \(b,\) when written in base \(10,\) equals
Solution:
Method 1: Use a place-value equation

Expressing both numerals by their place values turns the condition into an equation for the base. Since the digit \(5\) appears, \(b\) must be an integer with \(b\ge6\).

The values represented by \((24)_b\) and \((554)_b\) are \(2b+4\) and \(5b^2+5b+4\), respectively. Therefore
\[
(2b+4)^2=5b^2+5b+4.
\]
Expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
4b^2+16b+16=5b^2+5b+4,
\]
so
\[
b^2-11b-12=(b-12)(b+1)=0.
\]
Thus \(b=12\) or \(b=-1\). The latter is not an allowed base, whereas \(12\ge6\) makes every displayed digit valid. Hence \(\boxed{b=12}\), choice C.

Method 2: Use the units digit and carrying

The last digit sharply restricts the possible bases. First, \(b\) is an integer greater than \(5\), because \(5\) is one of the displayed digits.

When \((24)_b\) is squared, the units calculation is \(4\cdot4=16\). Every other place-value contribution is a multiple of \(b\). For the answer to end in \(4\), division of \(16\) by \(b\) must therefore leave remainder \(4\). Thus, for some nonnegative integer carry \(q\),
\[
16=qb+4,
\qquad qb=12.
\]
The only positive divisors of \(12\) greater than \(5\) are \(6\) and \(12\), so these are the only possible bases.

For \(b=6\),
\[
(24)_6=16,
\qquad (554)_6=5\cdot36+5\cdot6+4=214,
\]
and \(16^2=256\ne214\), so this base fails.

For \(b=12\),
\[
(24)_{12}=28,
\qquad (554)_{12}=5\cdot144+5\cdot12+4=784=28^2.
\]
This base satisfies the original condition. Therefore \(\boxed{b=12}\), choice C.
